vote.title: Voting in federal elections
vote.subtitle: Elections Canada · register, ID, ways to vote
vote.q.title: A few quick questions
vote.verdict.eligible: You can vote in federal elections.
vote.verdict.eligibleSub: Make sure you’re registered at your current address, so your voter information card comes to you when an election is called.
vote.verdict.future-elector: You can sign up now and be ready at 18.
vote.verdict.future-electorSub: Canadian citizens aged 14 to 17 can join the Register of Future Electors. You’re added to the list of electors when you turn 18.
vote.verdict.too-young: You can join the Register of Future Electors at 14.
vote.verdict.too-youngSub: It’s for Canadian citizens aged 14 to 17 who live in Canada. Voting starts at 18.
vote.verdict.not-citizen: Only Canadian citizens can vote in federal elections.
vote.verdict.not-citizenSub: Permanent residents and visitors can’t register or vote federally. Once you become a citizen and are 18 or older, you can register.
vote.verdict.abroad: You can vote by mail from abroad.
vote.verdict.abroadSub: Canadian citizens 18 or older who live outside Canada and have lived in Canada at some point can apply to the International Register of Electors. When an election is called, you get a special ballot by mail.
vote.verdict.unknown: To vote federally, you must be a Canadian citizen and at least 18.
vote.verdict.unknownSub: Answer the questions below to see what applies to you.
vote.tab.label: Voting topics
vote.later.title: When you’re 18
vote.later.sub: The ID to bring and the ways to vote
vote.reg.lead: Registering in advance means your voter information card arrives in the mail when an election is called. It tells you when, where and the ways to vote.
vote.reg.online: Check, update or complete your registration online
vote.reg.onlineDetail: Elections Canada’s Online Voter Registration Service. Use it after you move, too.
vote.reg.taxDetail: Answer the Elections Canada questions when you file with the Canada Revenue Agency, every year.
vote.reg.mailDetail: Contact Elections Canada and they’ll send you a form by mail, email or fax.
vote.reg.pollsDetail: During a general election or by-election, register at your local Elections Canada office or your polling place when you vote.
vote.reg.future: Join the Register of Future Electors
vote.reg.futureDetail: For Canadian citizens aged 14 to 17 living in Canada. Register online with Elections Canada.
vote.reg.abroad: Apply to the International Register of Electors
vote.reg.abroadDetail: For Canadian citizens 18 or older who live outside Canada and have lived in Canada at some point. You vote by special ballot, by mail.
vote.id.lead: At the polls you prove your identity and your address. Pick what you have:
vote.id.o1.title: One piece of ID
vote.id.o1.body: Your driver’s licence, or any Canadian government card with your photo, name and current address.
vote.id.o2.title: Two pieces of ID
vote.id.o2.body: Both with your name, and at least one with your current address. For example, a health card and a bank statement.
vote.id.o3.title: No ID
vote.id.o3.body: Declare your identity and address in writing, and have someone who knows you and is assigned to your polling station vouch for you.
vote.id.hint: Pick an option to see what to bring.
vote.id.result.o1: You’re set: show that one card at the polls.
vote.id.result.o2: You’re set: bring both pieces. Only one needs your current address.
vote.id.result.o3: You can still vote. Your voucher must prove their own identity and address, and can vouch for only one person (except in long-term care).
vote.id.ex.4: Student ID card or school letter
vote.id.tip.expired: Expired ID is fine if it shows your name and current address.
vote.id.tip.digital: E-statements and e-bills count: print them or show them on your phone.
vote.id.tip.passport: A passport proves who you are, not where you live.
vote.ways.lead: Once an election is called, you have four ways to vote. Each needs proof of identity and address.
vote.ways.day.title: On election day
vote.ways.day.body: At your assigned polling station. Your voter information card lists the address and hours.
vote.ways.advance.title: At advance polls
vote.ways.advance.body: On the 10th, 9th, 8th and 7th days before election day, at your assigned advance polling station.
vote.ways.office.title: At any Elections Canada office
vote.ways.office.body: Anywhere in the country, until the 6th day before election day (the Tuesday before).
vote.ways.mail.title: By mail
vote.ways.mail.body: Apply for a special ballot by 6 p.m. on the Tuesday before election day. Once accepted, it’s the only way you can vote.
vote.ways.note: Advance polls, offices and mail-in voting open only after an election is called.
vote.ready.title: Ready to vote
vote.ready.reg: Registration checked at my current address
vote.ready.regDetail: Online with Elections Canada, or on your tax return.
vote.ready.id: ID that proves my identity and address
vote.ready.idDetail: One card, two pieces, or a voucher.
vote.ready.plan: A plan for how I’ll vote
vote.ready.planDetail: Election day, advance polls, an office, or by mail.

vote.quebec.body: Provincial elections are run by Élections Québec, not Elections Canada. Check your provincial registration with them.

parl.parts.title: Three parts, one Parliament
parl.parts.crownBody: The Sovereign, represented by the Governor General, gives royal assent: the last step before a bill becomes law.
parl.parts.senateBody: {seats} senators study and improve bills. Every bill must pass the Senate to become law.
parl.parts.houseBody: {seats} seats, one for each riding. Bills about spending or taxes must start here.
parl.steps.title: How a bill becomes law
parl.step.noticeBody: 48 hours’ written notice before a bill is introduced.
parl.step.firstBody: The bill is introduced. There’s no debate at this stage.
parl.step.secondBody: MPs debate the bill’s main idea, then send it to a committee.
parl.step.committeeBody: A committee hears witnesses, studies it clause by clause and can amend it.
parl.step.reportBody: The House can propose more amendments.
parl.step.thirdBody: Final debate and vote on the bill as a whole.
parl.step.senateBody: The Senate follows similar steps. Both chambers must pass the same text.
parl.step.assentBody: The Governor General gives assent and the bill becomes law. It takes effect that day or on a date set in the act.

vote.verdict.future-abroad: You can apply to vote from abroad once you’re 18.
vote.verdict.future-abroadSub: The Register of Future Electors is for young citizens living in Canada. At 18, if you’ve lived in Canada at some point, you can apply to the International Register of Electors.
vote.reg.leadFuture: Sign up once now, and you’re added to the list of electors automatically when you turn 18.
vote.reg.leadAbroad: Once you’re on the International Register of Electors, a voting kit is mailed to you as soon as an election is called.
vote.reg.tooYoungInfo: Nothing to do yet. Once you join at 14, you’re added to the list of electors automatically when you turn 18.
vote.reg.futureAbroadInfo: Nothing to do yet. Canadian citizens 18 or older who live outside Canada and have lived in Canada at some point can apply to the International Register of Electors.
